cards.title: Abraham journeys to Canaan
cards.description: The Torah tells how Abraham left his home in Mesopotamia and traveled to Canaan. Jewish tradition honors him as the first of the patriarchs.
cards.meanwhile: In Egypt, the Great Pyramid of Giza had already stood for about 560 years.

cards.title: The Exodus from Egypt
cards.description: The Torah tells how the Israelites, led by Moses, left slavery in Egypt and traveled toward Canaan. Jews retell this story every year at Passover.

cards.title: The Merneptah Stele names Israel
cards.description: A stone monument set up by the Egyptian king Merneptah mentions a people called Israel living in Canaan. It is one of the earliest known written mentions of Israel.

cards.title: Villages rise in the hills of Canaan
cards.description: Between about 1200 and 1000 BCE, many small villages appeared in the hill country of Canaan. They are the communities of the early Israelites.

cards.title: David makes Jerusalem his capital
cards.description: The Bible tells how David became king and made Jerusalem his capital. Jerusalem became the center of Jewish life.
cards.meanwhile: In Peru, builders are raising the great temple center of Chavin de Huantar around 1000 BCE.

cards.title: Solomon builds the First Temple
cards.description: The Bible says King Solomon built the First Temple in Jerusalem. It became the holiest place in Jewish life.
cards.meanwhile: In Nigeria, the Nok people begin making clay sculptures around 900 BCE.

cards.title: The kingdom splits in two
cards.description: After Solomon, the Israelite kingdom divided. Israel was in the north, and Judah, with Jerusalem, was in the south.
cards.meanwhile: In Greece, legend says the city of Sparta is founded around 900 BCE.

cards.title: Neighbors write about the kingdom of Israel
cards.description: A stone monument from the nearby kingdom of Moab, the Mesha Stele, names Israel and its king Omri.

cards.title: Assyria conquers the kingdom of Israel
cards.description: The Assyrian empire conquered Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. Many people were taken to other parts of the Assyrian empire. Others stayed in the land.
cards.meanwhile: In Italy, legend says Romulus founds the city of Rome in 753 BCE.

cards.title: Assyria invades Judah and captures Lachish
cards.description: King Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah and captured the city of Lachish. Carvings in his palace show the siege. Jerusalem was not taken.
cards.meanwhile: In Greece, people begin writing with an alphabet by about 750 BCE.

cards.title: Hezekiah's Tunnel
cards.description: Workers cut a long tunnel under Jerusalem to bring water from a spring into the city. An ancient inscription describes the two teams of diggers meeting in the middle.

cards.title: The Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls
cards.description: Two tiny silver scrolls found in a burial cave in Jerusalem hold words from the Priestly Blessing. They are among the oldest known texts of the Bible.

cards.title: Babylon takes Judeans into exile
cards.description: The Babylonian army captured Jerusalem and took King Jehoiachin and many leading people to Babylonia.

cards.title: A Jewish community grows in Babylonia
cards.description: Judeans in Babylonia built homes, farmed and kept their traditions. Babylonia became a lasting center of Jewish life.

cards.title: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the First Temple
cards.description: After a long siege, the Babylonians burned Jerusalem and the First Temple. More Judeans were taken to Babylonia. Others stayed in Judah.
cards.meanwhile: In the Greek city of Miletus, the thinker Thales predicts a solar eclipse in 585 BCE that stops a battle between the Lydians and Medes.

cards.title: Cyrus the Great lets the Jews return
cards.description: In 539 BCE, the Persian king Cyrus the Great issued the Edict of Cyrus allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem and the Land of Judah, which was made a self-governing Jewish province under the new Persian Empire.
cards.meanwhile: In China, Confucius, the famous teacher, is born in 551 BCE.

cards.title: Second Temple completed
cards.description: The Jews who returned from Babylonia rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem. It was completed in 516 BCE and stood for nearly 600 years.
cards.meanwhile: In Greece, the city of Athens starts one of the first democracies in 508 BCE.

cards.title: A Jewish community on Elephantine
cards.description: Letters on papyrus from Elephantine, an island in the Nile in southern Egypt, show a Jewish community with its own temple. They asked leaders in Jerusalem for help to rebuild it.

cards.title: Alexandria grows into a great Jewish center
cards.description: After Ptolemy I took power in Egypt, many Judeans came to live there. Alexandria became one of the largest Jewish communities in the world.

cards.title: Jews settle in Cyrenaica
cards.description: Under the Ptolemies, Jewish families settled in Cyrenaica, in what is now Libya, and a lasting community grew there.

cards.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls are written
cards.description: Over several centuries, Jews wrote and copied hundreds of scrolls. They include some of the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.

cards.title: Jewish families resettled in Asia Minor
cards.description: King Antiochus III moved Jewish families from Babylonia to Lydia and Phrygia in Asia Minor. The historian Josephus records the story.

cards.title: The Maccabees revolt
cards.description: Jews led by Judah Maccabee rose up against King Antiochus IV, who had banned Jewish practice. In 164 BCE they took back the Temple and rededicated it, the story told at Hanukkah.
cards.meanwhile: In Egypt, priests honor their king with the decree that is carved on the Rosetta Stone in 196 BCE.

cards.title: Jews live in Rome
cards.description: Jews were living in Rome by about 150 BCE, long before Rome took control of Judea.

cards.title: Jews live on Cyprus
cards.description: Jewish communities lived on Cyprus during the Hellenistic and Roman periods.

cards.title: Rome takes control of Judea
cards.description: The Roman general Pompey captured Jerusalem. Judea came under Roman control, and some captives were taken to Rome.

cards.title: Romans destroy Jerusalem and the Second Temple
cards.description: The historian Josephus tells how Roman forces destroyed Jerusalem and the Second Temple. Many Jews were killed, and survivors were enslaved. Jewish communities elsewhere in the land carried on.
cards.meanwhile: In Italy, Mount Vesuvius erupts and buries the city of Pompeii in 79 CE.

cards.title: Alexandria's Jewish community devastated
cards.description: In 115 CE, Jews in Egypt and other Roman lands rose up against Roman rule. This is called the Diaspora Revolt. In Alexandria, attacks and the Roman crackdown killed many Jews and devastated the Jewish community.

cards.title: Cyrenaica's Jewish communities devastated
cards.description: In 115 CE, Jews rose up against Roman rule in what is called the Diaspora Revolt. Rome crushed the revolt with mass killing, and the Jewish communities of Cyrenaica were devastated.

cards.title: Cyprus's Jewish community destroyed and banned
cards.description: In 115 CE, Jews rose up against Roman rule in what is called the Diaspora Revolt, and the revolt spread to Cyprus. Jewish life on the island was devastated by killing. The Roman historian Cassius Dio reports that Jews were then banned from landing on Cyprus.

cards.title: Diaspora Revolt
cards.description: Beginning in Libya and spread to Egypt, Israel, Cyprus, and Babylon, forty-five years after the Temple's destruction and 15 years before the Bar Kokhba Revolt, Jews revolted against Roman Emperor Trajan contributing to Trajan's JewHate.
cards.meanwhile: In Britain, the Romans begin building Hadrian's Wall in 122 CE to guard the edge of their empire.

cards.title: The Bar Kokhba revolt
cards.description: Jews led by Shimon bar Kokhba rose up against Rome in Judea. Rome crushed the revolt in 135 CE and Judea suffered terribly. Jewish life continued, and the Galilee became its center.
cards.meanwhile: In China, Zhang Heng builds a bronze earthquake detector in 132 CE.

cards.title: The Mishnah is written down
cards.description: In the Galilee, Rabbi Judah the Prince gathered Jewish oral teachings into a written book, the Mishnah.
cards.meanwhile: In China, the Han dynasty, which ruled for about 400 years, ends in 220 CE.

cards.title: Babylonia is a leading center of Jewish life
cards.description: Under the Sasanian Persian Empire, Babylonia was one of the largest and most important Jewish centers in the world. Its Jewish scholars taught in great schools and shaped Jewish law and study for centuries.

cards.title: Alexandria's Jews are forced out
cards.description: In 415 CE, many of the Jews of Alexandria were forced to leave the city. Alexandria had been one of the greatest Jewish centers in the world for more than 700 years.

cards.title: Persia conquers Jerusalem
cards.description: In 614 CE, the Persian army of the Sasanian Empire captured Jerusalem from the Byzantine Empire. Jews continued to live in the Land under its new ruler.
cards.meanwhile: In China, the Sui dynasty begins building the Grand Canal in 605 CE to carry grain and travelers across the land.

cards.title: Jews live in Medina
cards.description: When Muhammad arrived in the city of Medina in 622 CE, large Jewish groups already lived there. At that time the city was called Yathrib.

cards.title: The Byzantines take back Jerusalem
cards.description: In 628 to 630 CE, the Byzantine Empire won back Jerusalem and the Land of Israel from Persia. It was another change of rulers for the Jews who lived there.
cards.meanwhile: In China, the monk Xuanzang sets out around 629 CE on a journey of about 16 years to India to bring back Buddhist books.

cards.title: Muslim armies conquer the Land of Israel
cards.description: Between 634 and 638 CE, Muslim armies conquered the Land of Israel from the Byzantine Empire. Jews continued to live in the Land under Muslim rule.
cards.meanwhile: In England, a ship filled with treasure is buried at Sutton Hoo around 625 CE.

cards.title: Muslim armies conquer Egypt
cards.description: In 641 and 642 CE, Muslim armies conquered Egypt, including the great city of Alexandria. Jewish communities there carried on under their new rulers.
cards.meanwhile: In Mexico, a boy of 12 named Pakal becomes ruler of the Maya city of Palenque in 615 CE.

cards.title: Muslim rule replaces Persian rule in Iraq
cards.description: Around 650 CE, Muslim rule replaced Sasanian Persian rule in Babylonia, now Iraq. The large Jewish community there kept its place as a leading center of Jewish life.
cards.meanwhile: In Japan, the Taika Reform of 645 CE gives the emperor more power over the land.

cards.title: Iraq stays a great center of Jewish learning
cards.description: From about 700 to 1100 CE, Iraq, the old land of Babylonia, remained one of the largest and most important Jewish centers in the world. Jewish leaders and teachers there were respected by Jews across the Muslim world.

cards.title: Jews live across Persia
cards.description: Between 700 and 1100 CE, Jewish communities spread across Persia, the land of modern Iran. They formed a wide network of towns and trade connections.

cards.title: Jewish life continues in the Land of Israel and Syria
cards.description: Jews continued to live in the Land of Israel and Syria after the Muslim conquest. Their communities carried on in towns and cities across the region.

cards.title: Egypt keeps a large Jewish community
cards.description: From 700 to 1100 CE, Egypt kept a large Jewish community. Its cities were home to Jewish families, scholars and merchants.

cards.title: Jewish life grows across North Africa
cards.description: From the 8th to the 11th century, the Maghreb, the lands of North Africa west of Egypt, grew into a large Jewish center. Many towns there had Jewish neighborhoods.

cards.title: Jewish life grows in al-Andalus
cards.description: In al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled part of Spain and Portugal, the Jewish population grew large and strong between 700 and 1100 CE. Jews there worked as scholars, doctors, merchants and officials.

cards.title: Jewish communities last in southern Italy and Sicily
cards.description: From 700 to 1100 CE, large Jewish communities lived in southern Italy and on the island of Sicily. They stayed there for centuries.

cards.title: Jewish towns appear across Central Asia
cards.description: By the 8th and 9th centuries, Jewish communities lived in Central Asia and Khorasan, along the old trade roads. Towns such as Balkh, Khwarezm and Merv had Jewish residents.

cards.title: Jews live in Yemen
cards.description: Jewish families kept living in Yemen from 700 to 1100 CE. Jews had already lived in Yemen for centuries before this time.

cards.title: Jewish communities in southern France
cards.description: From 700 to 1100 CE, Jews continued to live in the towns of southern France. Their communities stayed in the region for centuries.

cards.title: Ashkenazi Jews take root on the Rhine
cards.description: Between 700 and 1100 CE, a new Jewish population grew along the Rhine River and in Germany. These Jews are called Ashkenazi, from the Hebrew name for Germany.

cards.title: Muslim armies cross into Spain
cards.description: In 711 CE, Muslim armies crossed from North Africa into Iberia. Over the next years they took most of Spain and Portugal, and the Jewish communities there came under Muslim rule.
cards.meanwhile: In Japan, the city of Nara becomes the capital in 710 CE.

cards.title: Kairouan becomes a major Jewish center
cards.description: From about 800 to 1057 CE, the city of Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, was a major center of Jewish life in North Africa. Its Jewish community was known for its scholars and its trade.

cards.title: Jewish traders connect with western India
cards.description: By the 9th and 10th centuries, records show Jews living and trading in western India. They were part of the busy sea routes of the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Jews move from North Africa to Egypt
cards.description: Beginning around 900 CE, Jewish families moved from the Maghreb, in North Africa, to Egypt. They joined the Jewish communities already living in Egypt.

cards.title: Jews settle in Poland
cards.description: From the 11th to the 13th century, a Jewish presence grew in Poland. Jewish settlers, many from German lands, found new homes there.

cards.title: Jewish merchants link Egypt, Aden and India
cards.description: From about 1080 to 1240, Jewish merchants traded by sea between Egypt, Aden and India. Their letters and business papers were saved in the Cairo Geniza, a storeroom for old documents.

cards.title: Speyer's Jews are mostly protected
cards.description: In 1096, Crusaders attacked the Jews of Speyer in the Rhineland. Most of the community was protected, though some Jews were killed.

cards.title: Worms' Jewish community is devastated
cards.description: In 1096, Crusaders gathered in the Rhineland to march toward Jerusalem, and they attacked Jewish communities along the way. In Worms, many Jews were killed and the community was devastated. Jews later returned and rebuilt it.

cards.title: Mainz's Jewish community is devastated
cards.description: In May 1096, Crusaders attacked the Jews of Mainz, one of the great Jewish centers of the Rhineland. Many were killed, and the community was devastated. Jews later returned to Mainz and began again.

cards.title: The Rhineland communities recover and grow
cards.description: After the attacks of 1096, the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz were re-established and grew. They are known as the ShUM communities, a name made from the first letters of the three cities in Hebrew.

cards.title: Jewish communities spread across England
cards.description: In the 1100s and 1200s, Jewish communities lived in many English towns, not only in London. They lasted until the expulsion of 1290.

cards.title: Jewish life shrinks under the Almohads
cards.description: In 1148 CE, the Almohad rulers took control of parts of Spain and North Africa. Jews under their rule were pressed to convert, and the Jewish population shrank.

cards.title: France's king expels the Jews
cards.description: In 1182, King Philip II expelled the Jews from the royal lands of France. They were forced to leave their homes.

cards.title: York's Jewish community is destroyed
cards.description: In 1190, a mob attacked the Jews of York, England. Many Jews sought safety in a royal tower called Clifford's Tower, and most of them died there. The Jewish community of York was destroyed.

cards.title: Jews may return to the French royal lands
cards.description: In 1198, King Philip II of France allowed Jews to return to the lands he ruled directly. He had expelled them in 1182. Jewish life began again in the royal towns.

cards.title: Jews return to York
cards.description: In the early 1200s, Jews came back to York, and the community began again. It joined the other Jewish communities of England.

cards.title: The ShUM communities write shared rules
cards.description: Around 1220, the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz wrote shared rules for their communal life. These rules are called the ShUM ordinances.
cards.meanwhile: In England, King John signs Magna Carta in 1215 CE, a charter that limits the power of the king.

cards.title: The Disputation of Barcelona
cards.description: In 1263, King James I of Aragon ordered a public debate in Barcelona between the Jewish scholar Moses ben Nahman, called Nachmanides, and a Christian leader named Pablo Christiani. Nachmanides defended Judaism before the king.
cards.meanwhile: In Italy, 17-year-old Marco Polo leaves Venice in 1271 CE for a trip to China that lasts about 24 years.

cards.title: The Statute of Kalisz
cards.description: In 1264, Duke Boleslaw the Pious of Greater Poland issued the Statute of Kalisz. It gave Jews legal rights and protection, and it drew Jewish settlers to Poland.
cards.meanwhile: In Japan, a Mongol fleet lands near Hakata Bay in 1274 CE.

cards.title: England's Statute of the Jewry
cards.description: In 1275, King Edward I issued the Statute of the Jewry. It banned Jews from lending money at interest and pushed them toward farming and trade.
cards.meanwhile: In China, Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty in 1271 CE.

cards.title: England expels its Jews
cards.description: In 1290, King Edward I ordered all Jews to leave England. Jews who had lived there for more than 200 years went to France and to other lands across Europe.

cards.title: Jews move from German lands to Eastern Europe
cards.description: Beginning around 1300, many Jews moved from the German-speaking lands to eastern and central Europe. They went east to Poland and nearby lands and built new communities.

cards.title: Jewish life grows in Poland and Hungary
cards.description: In the 1300s and 1400s, Jewish communities in Poland and Hungary grew stronger. They became leading centers of Jewish life in Europe.

cards.title: France expels its Jews
cards.description: In 1306, King Philip IV ordered the Jews to leave the Kingdom of France. They scattered to many places.

cards.title: Jews are allowed back into France
cards.description: In 1315, the king of France allowed Jews to return to his kingdom after the expulsion of 1306. Some Jewish families came back and rebuilt their communities.

cards.title: France expels its Jews again
cards.description: In 1322, the Jews of France were expelled a second time. Some had returned after the expulsion of 1306.

cards.title: Black Death violence destroys Jewish communities
cards.description: During the Black Death of 1348 to 1351, mobs blamed Jews for the plague. Jewish communities in many European towns were attacked, and some were destroyed. Germany and Alsace suffered some of the worst violence.

cards.title: Violence destroys Jewish communities in Spain
cards.description: In 1391, mobs attacked Jewish quarters in cities across Spain. Many Jews were killed, some communities were destroyed, and many Jews were forced to convert. Some Jews fled to safer places.

cards.title: France expels its Jews once more
cards.description: In 1394, King Charles VI ordered the Jews out of France. It was the last of the French expulsions of the Middle Ages.

cards.title: The Vienna Gesera
cards.description: In 1420 and 1421, Duke Albert V of Austria had the Jews of Vienna arrested. Many were killed or driven out, and the medieval Jewish community of Vienna was destroyed. The event is called the Vienna Gesera, which means the Vienna decree.

cards.title: The Ottomans resettle Jews in Constantinople
cards.description: After the Ottoman Empire conquered Constantinople in 1453, the sultan ordered people from across his lands to settle in the city, including Jews. Jewish life in Constantinople, now also called Istanbul, grew again.

cards.title: Trent's Jewish community is destroyed
cards.description: In 1475, a Christian child named Simon was found dead in Trent, Italy, and Jews were falsely blamed. The Jews of Trent were arrested, and the community was destroyed.

cards.title: Spain expels its Jews
cards.description: In 1492, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella ordered the Jews of Spain to convert or leave. Many Jews left for Portugal, North Africa, Italy and the Ottoman lands.

cards.title: Sicily's Jews are expelled
cards.description: In 1492, the Jews of Sicily, which was ruled by the Spanish crown, were also expelled. They found new homes in several places.

cards.title: Portugal's Jews are forced to convert
cards.description: In 1496 and 1497, the king of Portugal ordered the Jews to become Christians. Most were forced to convert, and openly Jewish life in Portugal nearly ended.

cards.title: Jews from Iberia and Italy move to Ottoman cities
cards.description: From about 1500 to 1650, Jews from Spain, Portugal and Italy moved to cities of the Ottoman Empire. They settled in places such as Istanbul and Salonica and joined Jewish communities already there.

cards.title: Jews move to Safed and Jerusalem
cards.description: In the early and mid-1500s, Jews from around the Mediterranean moved to the Land of Israel. Many settled in Safed, and others in Jerusalem.

cards.title: Portuguese New Christians leave Iberia
cards.description: In the 1500s and 1600s, many New Christians from Portugal and Spain, Jews who had been forced to convert, left Iberia. They settled in Western Europe and around the Mediterranean, where many returned openly to Judaism.

cards.title: Jewish life grows in Istanbul and Salonica
cards.description: In the 1500s, Jewish newcomers settled in Istanbul, Salonica and the Ottoman Balkans. They joined Jewish communities that were already there, and these communities grew stronger.

cards.title: Safed grows into a Jewish center
cards.description: In the 1500s, the town of Safed, in the Galilee, grew into a major center of Jewish life. Its Jewish population grew a great deal.

cards.title: The Ottomans conquer the Land of Israel, Syria and Egypt
cards.description: In 1516 and 1517, the Ottoman Empire conquered Syria, the Land of Israel and Egypt. The Jews who lived there came under Ottoman rule.
cards.meanwhile: In Germany, a monk named Martin Luther posts his 95 Theses in 1517 CE.

cards.title: Venice orders Jews into the Ghetto
cards.description: In 1516, the city of Venice ordered its Jews to live in one walled area called the Ghetto. The gates were locked at night. The word ghetto comes from this place.
cards.meanwhile: In England, Thomas More publishes his book Utopia in 1516 CE, about an imaginary perfect island.

cards.title: The Inquisition begins in Portugal
cards.description: In 1536, Portugal set up its Inquisition, a church court that hunted for secret Jewish practice. New Christians, Jews who had been forced to convert, were its main targets.
cards.meanwhile: In India, Babur wins the Battle of Panipat in 1526 CE and founds the Mughal Empire.

cards.title: Rome orders its Jews into a ghetto
cards.description: In 1555, Pope Paul IV ordered the Jews of Rome to live in a walled ghetto. He also forced them to wear special hats or badges.
cards.meanwhile: In Russia, workers begin building Saint Basil's Cathedral in Moscow in 1555 CE.

cards.title: The popes expel Jews from most Papal lands
cards.description: In 1569 and 1593, popes ordered Jews out of most of the Papal States, the lands the Church ruled in Italy. Jews were allowed to stay in only a few cities, such as Rome.

cards.title: Jews travel to Amsterdam
cards.description: Around 1590, Jews from Portugal, Spain and other European ports began sailing to Amsterdam. They came as merchants and as families looking for a safer home.

cards.title: Livorno grows quickly
cards.description: In the 1590s, the rulers of Livorno, a port in Italy, offered special privileges to attract merchants, including Jews. The Jewish community there grew rapidly.

cards.title: A Portuguese Jewish community begins in Amsterdam
cards.description: Around 1590, Portuguese Jews began to settle in Amsterdam, in the Dutch Republic. Many came from families that had been forced to convert in Portugal. They formed an openly Jewish community.

cards.title: Ashkenazi Jews come to Amsterdam
cards.description: In the early 1600s, Jews from Central and Eastern Europe, called Ashkenazim, also began to settle in Amsterdam. They lived alongside the Portuguese Jews who had arrived earlier.

cards.title: Suriname has a growing Jewish community
cards.description: In the 1600s, a Jewish community grew in Suriname, on the northern coast of South America, and about 570 Jews lived there in 1694. That year, about 40 sugar plantations owned mostly by Jews were worked by about 9,000 enslaved Africans. Slavery was central to the colony's economy, and planters of many backgrounds took part in it.

cards.title: Jews settle in Barbados
cards.description: In the 1600s, Jews built an established community on the island of Barbados. It was one of several Caribbean islands where Jewish communities took root.

cards.title: Jews sail from Amsterdam to Dutch Brazil
cards.description: Starting in the 1630s, Jews sailed from Amsterdam and the Atlantic world to Dutch-ruled Brazil. Many settled in Recife, where they built a Jewish community. Ships now linked Amsterdam, the Mediterranean and Brazil.

cards.title: The first Jewish community in the Americas
cards.description: In the 1630s, Jews in Recife, in Dutch-ruled Brazil, formed the first openly organized Jewish community in the Americas. It lasted until 1654, when Portugal took the town back.

cards.title: Khmelnytsky's uprising devastates Jewish towns
cards.description: In 1648, a Cossack uprising led by Bohdan Khmelnytsky swept across Ukraine and nearby lands. Jewish communities were attacked, many Jews were killed, and some towns were destroyed. Jews who survived often fled to safer places.

cards.title: Jewish life in Poland-Lithuania recovers
cards.description: After the destruction of the 1640s and 1650s, the Jewish population of Poland-Lithuania recovered and grew. A census-based count of 1764 and 1765 shows about 750,000 Jews.

cards.title: Curaçao's Jewish community grows
cards.description: Jews began settling on the island of Curaçao in 1651, and the Mikvé Israel congregation was founded in 1659. Curaçao grew into one of the major Jewish centers of the Caribbean.

cards.title: The Jews of Recife are scattered
cards.description: In 1654, Portugal took Recife back from the Dutch, and the Jews of Recife had to leave. Most returned to Amsterdam, and others went to the Caribbean, including Curaçao. One small group of 23 reached New Amsterdam, now New York.

cards.title: Jews reach New Amsterdam
cards.description: In September 1654, 23 Jewish refugees arrived in New Amsterdam, now New York City. They had fled Recife after Portugal took it back. Governor Peter Stuyvesant opposed them, but Dutch West India Company leaders let them stay.

cards.title: Jamaica's Jewish community grows
cards.description: After 1655, when England took Jamaica from Spain, the Jewish community on the island grew. Jamaica became another Caribbean home for Jewish families.

cards.title: Jews return to England
cards.description: In 1655 and 1656, England quietly allowed Jews to live there openly again, more than 360 years after the expulsion of 1290. A Jewish community began to grow in London.

cards.title: Jews settle in Newport
cards.description: In 1658, Jews began settling in Newport, Rhode Island. Their community later built the Touro Synagogue, which still stands today.

cards.title: Sabbatai Zevi
cards.description: In 1666, the Ottoman sultan arrested Sabbatai Zevi, a man many Jews believed was the Messiah. Under pressure, he converted to Islam. Hopes among Jews across Europe and the Middle East were shattered.
cards.meanwhile: In London, the Great Fire burns much of the city in 1666 CE.

cards.title: Vienna expels its Jews
cards.description: In 1669 and 1670, Emperor Leopold I ordered the Jews of Vienna to leave. Jewish families were forced out of the city.

cards.title: Jews settle in Charleston
cards.description: A Jewish resident of Charleston, South Carolina, is documented in 1695. In 1749, the community organized the congregation Kahal Kadosh Beth Elohim. Around 1800, about 500 Jews lived in Charleston.

cards.title: Hasidism begins to spread
cards.description: In the 1700s, a new Jewish movement called Hasidism rose in Eastern Europe. It stressed joy, prayer and closeness to God.
cards.meanwhile: In Russia, Tsar Peter the Great founds the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703 CE.

cards.title: Savannah's first Jewish settlers arrive
cards.description: In July 1733, 42 Jews arrived in Savannah, Georgia, aboard a ship called the William and Sarah. They were among the first settlers of the new colony.

cards.title: A Jewish community forms in Philadelphia
cards.description: Beginning in the 1740s, Jewish families formed a community in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It grew into one of the main Jewish centers of colonial America.

cards.title: Prague's Jews are expelled
cards.description: In 1744, Empress Maria Theresa ordered the Jews out of Prague. They were allowed to return in 1748.

cards.title: Jews return to Prague
cards.description: In 1748, Jews were allowed back into Prague after being expelled in 1744. They returned and rebuilt their community.

cards.title: The partitions of Poland
cards.description: From 1772 to 1795, Russia, Prussia and Austria divided up Poland. Jewish towns stayed where they were, but their Jewish residents now lived under new rulers.

cards.title: Hasidic Jews move to Safed
cards.description: In 1777, a group of about 300 Hasidic Jews from Belarus and Lithuania traveled to the Land of Israel. They settled in Safed.

cards.title: Joseph II of Austria eases rules for Jews
cards.description: In 1782, Emperor Joseph II of Austria issued Toleration Patents that eased some limits on Jews. Jews gained more freedom to study, work and trade.
cards.meanwhile: In France, the first people fly in a hot-air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers in 1783 CE.

cards.title: France gives its Jews citizenship
cards.description: In 1791, revolutionary France gave Jews full rights as citizens. France was the first major European nation to do so.
cards.meanwhile: In Haiti, enslaved people begin the uprising in 1791 CE that wins the country its freedom.

cards.title: The Jewish population of the Pale grows fast
cards.description: In the 1800s, the Jewish population of the Russian Empire grew dramatically. Most of these Jews lived in the Pale of Settlement.

cards.title: Jews move to Odessa and other big cities
cards.description: In the 1800s, many Jews left small towns in the Pale of Settlement and moved to Odessa and other large cities. They went to find work and new opportunities.

cards.title: Baghdadi Jews move to India
cards.description: In the 1800s, Jewish merchants and families from Baghdad and other parts of the Middle East moved to India. They built communities in cities such as Bombay and Calcutta.

cards.title: Odessa becomes a major Jewish center
cards.description: In 1851, about 17,000 Jews lived in Odessa, a port on the Black Sea. By 1892, there were more than 124,000. Odessa had become one of the major Jewish centers of the Russian Empire.

cards.title: Baghdadi Jews build communities in Bombay and Calcutta
cards.description: In the 1800s, Jews from Baghdad and nearby lands settled in the Indian port cities of Bombay and Calcutta. Their communities grew stronger with trade.

cards.title: Morocco is a major Jewish center
cards.description: In the 1800s, Morocco was one of the major centers of Jewish life. Many Moroccan Jews lived in walled Jewish quarters called mellahs.

cards.title: Jews remain strong in Yemen and Aden
cards.description: Jewish communities in Yemen and in the port of Aden continued through the 1800s and grew stronger. Yemen's Jews had lived in the region for many centuries.

cards.title: Russia sets the borders of the Pale of Settlement
cards.description: In 1804 and 1835, Russia set the borders of the Pale of Settlement, the region where most Jews were allowed to live. Jews needed special permission to live outside it. Russia had been limiting where Jews could settle since 1791.
cards.meanwhile: In France, Napoleon crowns himself emperor in 1804 CE.

cards.title: The Perushim move to the Land of Israel
cards.description: In 1808, a group of Jews called the Perushim began moving from Lithuania and Belarus to the Land of Israel. They were followers of the great scholar known as the Vilna Gaon.

cards.title: Jews from Central Europe move to the United States
cards.description: Beginning around 1820, many Jews moved from Central Europe to the United States. They came to find work and a better life.

cards.title: The Jewish population of the United States grows
cards.description: In 1820, about 3,000 Jews lived in the United States. By 1880, as many as 300,000 lived there.

cards.title: Safed is attacked and plundered
cards.description: In 1834, attackers plundered Safed and robbed its Jews. The Jewish community lost people and property, but it survived.

cards.title: An earthquake strikes Safed
cards.description: On January 1, 1837, a powerful earthquake destroyed much of Safed. Many of those who died were Jews, and the community shrank. It survived and began to rebuild.

cards.title: Mashhad's Jews are forced to convert
cards.description: In 1839, a mob attacked the Jewish quarter of Mashhad, in Persia, and killed about 32 Jews. The roughly 2,000 Jews who remained were forced to convert to Islam outwardly. Many kept their Jewish traditions in secret.

cards.title: The Damascus Affair
cards.description: In 1840, Jewish leaders in Damascus were arrested and tortured after they were falsely accused of murdering a Christian monk. Jewish leaders around the world spoke out, and the accused were freed.
cards.meanwhile: In Britain, the world's first postage stamp, the Penny Black, goes on sale in 1840 CE.

cards.title: Jewish merchants move from India to Shanghai
cards.description: Beginning in 1845, Jewish merchants from India moved to Shanghai to trade. Many belonged to Baghdadi families.

cards.title: Shanghai gets a lasting Jewish community
cards.description: Beginning in 1845, Jewish merchants settled in Shanghai, China. Their community lasted and grew.

cards.title: Ottoman Jews gain equal rights
cards.description: Between 1856 and 1869, the Ottoman Empire passed reforms that made Jews and other non-Muslims equal citizens under the law. This was part of a wider set of Ottoman reforms called the Tanzimat.
cards.meanwhile: In Egypt, the Suez Canal opens in 1869 CE, linking the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea.

cards.title: Jews can sit in the British Parliament
cards.description: In 1858, Britain removed the last barrier that kept Jews from sitting in Parliament. Lionel de Rothschild, who had been elected years earlier, could finally take his seat.
cards.meanwhile: In 1858, the first telegraph message crosses the Atlantic Ocean by undersea cable, from Britain to North America.

cards.title: Jews build outside Jerusalem's Old City walls
cards.description: In 1860, Mishkenot Sha'ananim became the first Jewish neighborhood built outside the walls of Jerusalem's Old City. Jerusalem soon began to spread beyond its walls.

cards.title: The Alliance Israélite Universelle is founded
cards.description: In 1860, Jewish leaders in France founded the Alliance Israélite Universelle. It worked to protect Jewish rights and to open schools for Jews around the world.
cards.meanwhile: In Italy, Giuseppe Garibaldi leads about 1,000 volunteers in 1860 CE to help unite the country.

cards.title: Jews gain equal rights in Central Europe
cards.description: Between 1867 and 1871, Austria-Hungary, Germany and Italy gave Jews equal rights as citizens. Jews could now enter more schools and professions.
cards.meanwhile: In North America, Canada becomes a country in 1867 CE.

cards.title: The Crémieux Decree
cards.description: In 1870, France's Crémieux Decree made the Jews of Algeria French citizens. Adolphe Crémieux, a French Jewish lawyer and politician, helped write it.
cards.meanwhile: In Russia, Dmitri Mendeleev publishes his periodic table of the elements in 1869 CE.

cards.title: Petah Tikva is founded
cards.description: In 1878, Jewish settlers founded Petah Tikva, a farming village. The first settlement collapsed within a few years, but the village was later settled again.

cards.title: About 25,000 Jews live in the Land of Israel
cards.description: By 1880, about 23,000 to 26,000 Jews lived in the Land of Israel. Jews had lived there for thousands of years, long before the First Aliyah began.

cards.title: The Bene Israel are established in western India
cards.description: By 1880, the Bene Israel, a Jewish community in western India, were firmly established. They lived mainly in the Konkan region and in Bombay.

cards.title: Britain, Canada and South Africa gain Jewish communities
cards.description: From 1881 to 1914, large numbers of Jews from Eastern Europe settled in Britain, Canada and South Africa. Their Jewish communities grew quickly.

cards.title: Pogroms strike Jewish towns in Russia
cards.description: From 1881 to 1884, mobs attacked Jewish towns across the Russian Empire in violent riots called pogroms. Homes and shops were destroyed. The attacks led many Jews to leave.

cards.title: Eastern European Jews move to America
cards.description: Starting in 1881, huge numbers of Jews left Eastern Europe for the United States. More than 200,000 arrived in the 1880s and more than 300,000 in the 1890s, according to the Library of Congress.

cards.title: Yemenite Jews travel to Jerusalem and Jaffa
cards.description: In 1881 and 1882, about 200 Jews from Yemen traveled to the Land of Israel. They went to Jerusalem and Jaffa.

cards.title: The First Aliyah
cards.description: In 1882, the First Aliyah began. Over about 20 years, around 30,000 Jews, from Eastern Europe and Yemen, moved to the Land of Israel. Aliyah means going up in Hebrew.

cards.title: New farming villages rise in the Land of Israel
cards.description: Starting in 1882, Jewish settlers founded new farming villages in the Land of Israel. These villages strengthened the Jewish population already living there.

cards.title: Jews sail from Eastern Europe to Argentina
cards.description: Beginning in 1889, Jews from Eastern Europe sailed to Argentina to start new lives. The first organized group of 820 Russian Jews arrived that year.

cards.title: Argentina's Jewish farming colonies grow
cards.description: In 1889, Jewish farming colonies began in Argentina. The Jewish population there grew rapidly in the years that followed.

cards.title: Bukharan Jews move to Jerusalem
cards.description: In the late 1800s, Jews from Bukhara traveled across Central Asia to Jerusalem. Many settled in the city and formed a community of their own.

cards.title: The Jewish Colonization Association is founded
cards.description: In 1891, Baron Maurice de Hirsch founded the Jewish Colonization Association. It helped Jews from Eastern Europe settle as farmers in places such as Argentina.
cards.meanwhile: In Russia, workers begin building the Trans-Siberian Railway in 1891 CE, the longest railway in the world.

cards.title: The Bukharan Quarter is built in Jerusalem
cards.description: In 1892, Jews from Bukhara, in Central Asia, founded the Bukharan Quarter in Jerusalem. It added to the Jewish population of the city.

cards.title: The Dreyfus Affair
cards.description: In 1894, Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish army officer in France, was falsely convicted of treason. The case divided France and showed how strong anti-Jewish feeling remained.
cards.meanwhile: In Greece, the first modern Olympic Games open in Athens in 1896 CE.

cards.title: The First Zionist Congress
cards.description: In August 1897, Theodor Herzl brought Jewish leaders to Basel, Switzerland, for the first Zionist Congress. They aimed to create a Jewish homeland in the Land of Israel.
cards.meanwhile: In France, the Lumière brothers show movies to a paying audience for the first time in 1895 CE.

eras.name: Babylonia, Byzantium and the Islamic world
eras.summary: From the Mishnah at 200 CE through the Persian, Byzantine and Muslim conquests, Jewish life centers on Babylonia, Egypt, North Africa and al-Andalus.

eras.name: Medieval Europe and Iberia
eras.summary: Jewish communities grow in the Rhineland, France, England and Poland, but are attacked and expelled again and again, and many move east.

eras.name: Expulsions and the new diasporas
eras.summary: After Spain expels its Jews in 1492, Jews build new communities in Ottoman cities, Safed, Amsterdam and the Americas.

eras.name: Eastern Europe, new rights and mass migration
eras.summary: Hasidism spreads and the Pale of Settlement grows, Jews gain legal rights in Western and Central Europe, and large numbers move to America and the Land of Israel, until the First Zionist Congress in 1897.
